title: Electrical control of the metal-insulator transition in a one dimensional device
authors: J. Craquelin, L. Jarjat, B. Hue, A. Théry, C. Fruy, N. Struchkov, D. Stefani, M. M. Desjardins, A. Cottet, M. R. Delbecq, T. Kontos
abstract: Controlling the low energy spectrum at the nanoscale with an external physical parameter has become an important resource for quantum devices. The emergence of an energy gap is one such key feature, linked to the mitigation of decoherence needed for quantum information processing. Indeed, the detrimental effects of high-energy uncontrolled excitations can only be cured at some specific tuning points in general. Achieving an energy gap is a natural way to extend decoherence countermeasures over a finite region of parameter space. This would be particularly useful in view of the recent efforts to build superconducting topological chains in a top-down approach. In this work, we demonstrate a large energy gap by spatially modulating the local potential of a suspended carbon nanotube, exploiting an analogy with condensed matter systems. This gap is homogeneous on the nanotube and tunable by about two orders of magnitude, bringing the electronic system from an insulating state to a near-metallic state at low temperatures.
summary: The researchers show how applying patterned gate voltages can electrically induce a large, tunable energy gap in a one-dimensional carbon nanotube, effectively controlling its transition between metallic and insulating states. By modeling this using Mathieu's equation, they confirm that the gap opening is a single-particle effect controllable by the modulation strength. This technique offers a powerful tool for engineering quantum materials at the nanoscale.
main_problem: The work demonstrates electrical control over the metal-insulator transition (MIT) in a one-dimensional nanoscale device by inducing and tuning a large energy gap.
main_result: A sizable, homogeneous energy gap ($E_g \approx 5	ext{ meV}$) can be opened and tuned across two orders of magnitude simply by spatially modulating the local potential using external gates.
method: The study combines transport measurements (differential conductance mapping) with theoretical modeling based on solving the Schrödinger equation for a cosine-modulated potential, leading to Mathieu's equation.
model_or_system: The physical system is a suspended carbon nanotube patterned over multiple individually controlled gates. The underlying model treats the electronic structure as being governed by an effective periodic potential, analogous to the Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) chain or a cosine potential solved via Mathieu functions.
key_observables: Differential conductance ($G_{	ext{diff}}$) maps showing transitions between metallic and insulating states; the magnitude of the energy gap ($E_g$).
important_parameters: Gate modulation amplitude ($\Delta V_g$), temperature ($\approx 30	ext{ mK}$), and the periodicity/wavelength of the potential modulation.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes a non-interacting electron picture, simplifying the full Poisson-Schrödinger problem to an effective single-particle Hamiltonian solvable by Mathieu functions or tight-binding diagonalization.
figures_summary: Figures show differential conductance maps comparing weak vs. strong gate modulation, illustrating the transition from conductive (metallic) to gapped (insulating) behavior; theoretical plots confirm gap opening based on the modulated potential strength.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the experimental setup and observing the MIT via transport measurements, then developing a theoretical framework using Mathieu's equation to model the gate-induced periodic potential, culminating in quantitative agreement between theory (including disorder) and experiment.
why_interesting: This work provides an excellent platform for studying fundamental concepts like topological transitions and gap engineering in mesoscopic systems, which are highly relevant to realizing robust quantum components.
